Brutal Attack Upon a Lady.
The Oxford Lady.
The Oxford Ledger of Friday says: At Green's Station, on the O. & C. Railroad, Saturday morning Mrs. John L. Hall, one of the good ladies of that thriving village, was brutally assaulted in her own yard by a negro woman named Lyon and badly beaten. It seems that the daughter of this colored woman had been in the habit of passing through Mr. Hall's yard and had been repeatedly warned by Mrs H. not to do so, but she did not heed the warning. On Saturday she tried it again and was overhauled by Mrs Hall, who attempted to eject her from the premises when the Lyon woman suddenly appeared upon the scene with a stick in hand and commenced beating Mrs. Hall and continued until she had seriously beaten her prostrate victim. While the Lyon woman was administering heavy blows upon the head of Mrs. Hall her daughter who was some distance away heard the cries of her mother and ran to her assistance, but on her way she was seized by Monroe Lyon, the husband of the negro woman, and held until her mother was severely beaten and at the mercy of this miserable gang of negroes. The infuriated colored woman was not satisfied on Saturday

so sought her opportunity Sunday during the absence of Mr. Hall and made the second attack upon Mrs. Hall, and succeeded in striking her again over the head several times with a tobacco stick.

The negroes have all been arrested and great excitement exists in the neigeborhnod. They will be tried before 'Squire J. D. Tilley on Saturday.

Monroe Lyon has suffered the penalty for holding Miss Hall when she was on her way to rescue her mother from the foul attack of Lyon's wife, as he was taken out that night by unknown parties and severely whipped.

The Doctors Are Puzzled. EASTBOURNE, August 3.—Thomas Wickers, a tradesman established here, has just astonished the medical world. Sometime ago he made a curious attempt at suicide by driving four long nails into his head with a hammer. They penetrated into his brain to the extent of three inches and were withdrawn with great diffidulty. To the amazement of the doctors Wickers has completely recovered from his self-inflicted injuries and is able to attend to his business as he used. The doctors pronounce the case as being unparalleled in medical annals. Sensation at Green's Station.
The Durham Globe says: A gentleman from Green's station informed the reporter yesterday that the excitement occasioned by the beating of Mrs. Hall by a negro woman has not subsided. The woman and her children have left the neighborhood, but her husband is disabled by the severe whipping he received though none of his bones were broken. Five men were arrested for whipping him, but the hearing was postponed until next Saturday.

Lawrence county, Tennessee, is planning a monument to Davy Crockett, who began his remarkable career at Lawrenburg as a justice of the peace and ended it in glory at the Alamo, Texas. He was a famous backwoodsman, a unique border soldier and a politician of a peculiar and striking type. It was he who said, "Be sure you are right and then go ahead." Give him a monument. He deserves it.

VIGILANTS REPULSED.
Last Friday night Tom Chambers, colored, living on the Tennessee side of Fulton, was visited by a vigilance committee. Chambers went to the door to find out what they wanted, when the men grabbed at him. He eluded their grasp and picked up a hatchet with which to defend himself. He hit one of his assailants two or three times with the hatchet, and says the fellow acted like a chicken with its head cut off. Another one of them attacked Chambers, who drew out his knife and thrust it into him. The next morning the cause of the visit was ascertained by the finding of a rope with a hangman's knot in it. Chambers says the men were white and that he knows them. Chambers is the darkey who testified against some merchants in Fulton, who were arrested for selling whisky illegally. We understand he has given the Tennessee officials the names of the "lynch gang," and that he will have them arrested. However, as yet nothing has been done.—Fulton Argus.
